questions.title: What is Wasp, the full-stack web framework, and when would you choose it over a conventional React and Node app?
questions.quick: Wasp is a full-stack web framework where a declarative configuration file describes the app, such as pages, routes, queries, actions, authentication and jobs, and it generates glue code around React, Node.js and Prisma. It is not related to OWASP or WebAssembly projects with similar names. I would choose it for small teams building a conventional web app quickly and accepting the framework's conventions. For heavy customisation or organisation-wide standards I would use plain React and Node. I would verify current features at wasp.sh/docs.
questions.revision: Wasp: declarative config plus React, Node.js and Prisma with generated glue, for fast conventional apps; choose plain React and Node when you need full control or established standards.
questions.detailed:
**Check the official Wasp documentation at wasp.sh/docs for current features and version status.** Do not confuse it with unrelated projects that share the acronym, such as security or WebAssembly initiatives.

## What it is

Wasp is a framework for building full-stack web applications. You describe the application in a **declarative configuration** (pages, routes, data operations, authentication, background jobs) and write React components and Node.js server functions as usual. Wasp compiles this into a working client and server, wiring things like routing, auth and operations, with **Prisma** for the database layer.

## What it gives you

- Less boilerplate for auth, routing and client-server calls.
- A convention-based structure, helpful for small teams and newcomers.
- Familiar building blocks (React, Node.js, Prisma) rather than a proprietary UI model.

## When to choose it

| Situation | Wasp | Conventional React + Node |
|---|---|---|
| Small team, new internal tool or prototype | Strong fit | More setup |
| Standard CRUD, auth, jobs | Strong fit | Fine |
| Need unusual server architecture or protocols | Possible friction | Better |
| Organisation-wide platform standards | Check fit carefully | Better aligned |
| Hiring or onboarding with existing framework knowledge | Smaller pool | Larger pool |
| Long-term maintainability risk | Depends on project maturity | Lower |

## Evaluation checklist

1. Run a time-boxed spike: build one real feature end to end.
2. Check how to **escape** conventions (custom server code, own middleware).
3. Review release cadence, community activity and upgrade path.
4. Confirm deployment fits your hosting and security constraints.
5. Confirm testing works with your usual tools.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing it because it is fashionable, with no spike.
- Assuming generated code needs no understanding.
- Mixing it up with similarly named projects when searching.
- Ignoring lock-in and upgrade effort.
followUps: How would you spike Wasp in two days?
What would you do if you outgrew its conventions?
How does its auth compare with using an identity provider directly?

questions.title: How do you structure a React and TypeScript application that integrates with Dataverse or Microsoft Graph?
questions.quick: I keep authentication, API access and UI separate. MSAL handles sign-in with the authorization code flow and PKCE; tokens stay in the library's managed cache. For sensitive or complex integrations I put a backend-for-frontend in front of Dataverse or Graph so secrets and broad scopes stay on the server. A typed API client wraps calls with generated or hand-written types, central error handling and retry rules. Error boundaries and clear loading and error states protect the user experience. Scopes stay minimal and are verified in current documentation.
questions.revision: MSAL with code flow and PKCE, minimal scopes, optional backend-for-frontend, typed API client with central error handling, error boundaries and tested loading and error states.
questions.detailed:
## Layered structure

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| UI components | Render state, no direct HTTP or token logic |
| Feature hooks (for example data-fetching hooks) | Orchestrate queries, caching, optimistic updates |
| API client | Typed functions, base URL, headers, retries, error mapping |
| Auth module | MSAL configuration, sign-in, silent token acquisition |
| Types | Models for entities, ideally generated from schema or metadata |

## Authentication

- Use MSAL with the authorization code flow and PKCE for single-page apps; do not use the implicit flow.
- Request **only the scopes needed**, and prefer incremental consent.
- Acquire tokens silently per call; handle interaction-required errors by redirecting.
- Avoid storing tokens yourself; understand the cache location trade-offs in the library documentation.
- Verify current MSAL and Dataverse or Graph scope guidance in Microsoft Learn.

## Backend-for-frontend

{{diagram:bff}}

A BFF is worthwhile when you need to hide secrets, aggregate several calls, apply server-side authorisation, use the on-behalf-of flow, or limit what the browser can request. For simple, user-delegated reads, calling the API directly from the SPA can be acceptable.

## Typed client and errors

- Define response types; validate at the boundary if data is untrusted (a schema validator helps).
- Map HTTP errors to domain errors: unauthorised, throttled, not found, conflict.
- Respect throttling headers and back off.
- Use **error boundaries** for rendering failures, and explicit error states for data failures; do not rely on boundaries for network errors.

## Common mistakes

- Granting the app broad scopes "for convenience".
- Scattering fetch calls and token code across components.
- Using `any` for API responses.
- Ignoring throttling and pagination limits.
- No tests for token expiry and failed calls.

diagrams.title: React app with a backend-for-frontend
diagrams.alt: The React application signs in the user with MSAL and calls a backend-for-frontend with an access token. The backend validates the token, applies authorisation, and calls Dataverse or Microsoft Graph, using an on-behalf-of exchange where appropriate. Results return through the backend to the typed client in the app.

nodes.label: React app and typed API client

followUps: When would you skip the backend-for-frontend?
How do you handle token expiry during a long form edit?
How would you generate TypeScript types for Dataverse tables?

questions.title: Full-stack framework or separate frontend and backend for an enterprise internal tool: how do you decide?
questions.quick: I decide on team skills, lifetime of the tool, integration needs and exit cost. A full-stack framework gives speed and consistency for a small team with a conventional app. Separate frontend and backend suit multiple clients, shared APIs, independent scaling or teams, and strict enterprise standards. I look at escape hatches, testing, deployment fit and lock-in, and I run a short spike before committing. For an internal tool with a short horizon, speed often wins; for a platform others will integrate with, I separate.
questions.revision: Full-stack framework for speed with a small team and conventional needs; separate layers for multiple clients, independent teams and standards. Check escape hatches, testing, deployment, lock-in.
questions.detailed:
## Decision factors

| Factor | Full-stack framework | Separate frontend and backend |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first release | Faster | Slower initially |
| Team shape | One small team, mixed skills | Specialist teams, clear contracts |
| Number of clients | One web app | Web, mobile, partners, agents |
| Consistency | Framework conventions | Must be defined and enforced |
| Lock-in | Higher if conventions are deep | Lower; swap either side |
| Escape hatches | Check how to drop to custom code | Natural |
| Testing | Depends on framework tooling | Standard per layer |
| Deployment | Often one unit | Two pipelines, more flexibility |
| Scaling | Together | Independently |
| Security review | One surface | Clear API boundary to review |

## Questions to ask

1. Who will maintain it in three years, and what do they know?
2. Will anything other than this UI need the data or logic (reports, integrations, AI agents)? If yes, a real API boundary helps.
3. What does the organisation already standardise: identity, logging, hosting, CI?
4. How hard is it to leave the framework? Can business logic live in plain modules?
5. Does the framework's testing story fit our pipeline?

## Mitigations

- Keep business logic in framework-independent modules.
- Put an API contract (OpenAPI or similar) around anything others may call.
- Run a time-boxed spike on a real feature, including a deployment to the target environment.
- Record the decision and the conditions that would reverse it.

{{diagram:decide}}

## Common mistakes

- Choosing separate layers by default for a tiny tool, adding cost without benefit.
- Choosing a full-stack framework and letting logic leak into view code.
- Ignoring operational standards such as single sign-on and logging.
- Not documenting why the choice was made.

diagrams.title: Framework versus separate layers
diagrams.alt: The decision considers whether multiple clients or consumers need the API, then whether independent teams or scaling are needed, then whether a short spike shows the framework fits deployment and testing. Positive answers to the first two lead to separate layers, otherwise a full-stack framework is chosen when the spike passes.

followUps: How would you keep business logic portable inside a full-stack framework?
What would make you split a full-stack app later?
How do you decide who owns the API contract?
